newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Tsumeb security staff, manager still trapped.
newsitem.headline: Tsumeb security staff, manager still trapped.

text.p: Up to 30 security workers and their dogs at Namibian copper mine Tsumeb Corp Ltd (TSL) are trapped by armed strikers and have been without food since Monday, mine manager Tony de Beer told Reuters on Wednesday.
He said that the 25-30 security workers had been blockaded by armed members of the Mineworkers' Union of Namibia (MUN) at the Tsumeb site since last Thursday.
The union has said that the workers can leave, but only if they submit a list of their names. Strikers have not allowed food into the mine, de Beer said.

Mediation efforts to end the bitter six-week old dispute broke down last Thursday and the strike took a violent twist over the weekend when armed strikers gained control of the group's three mines -- Otjihase, Kombat and Tsumeb.
Namibian government ministers on Wednesday visited Kombat and Tsumeb to ask the strikers to put down their weapons. They had visited Otjihase on Tuesday.

But the pleas from the Minister of Mines and the Minister of Labour did not succeeed. A spokesman for mine-owner Gold Fields of Namibia said the situation had not changed and armed strikers were still in control of all three mines.
"Nothing has changed," he said, describing the atmosphere as "terribly, terribly tense".

The strike over pay began with TCL offering a seven percent rise and the union wanting 14.5 percent. A new pay offer is to be put forward by Friday aimed at settling the dispute or, at least, starting mediation again.
Tsumeb mines and smelters have been shut down since August 23 when MUN members began to strike.
The strike is costing TCL some 80 tonnes a day in lost copper production and a similar amount in lost lead.
TCL produced just under 30,000 tonnes of blister copper last year and 27,000 tonnes of lead. Most of the lead was produced from bought-in material while copper output was from TCL mines.
